title: The tellers close
hookLine: a scribe and a poet, both servants of the Word

lines: A PEN WRITING OUT THE HYMNS.
A CAREFUL HAND, A BURNING HEART.
cards: Two men who never needed to meet to belong together. One is bent over a page, pen in hand, writing out the Guru's hymns as Guru Arjan dictates, tradition says, and adding nothing of his own.
The other sits at Guru Gobind Singh's court, writing Persian verses of longing for the Beloved. A careful hand and a burning heart. Different languages, different generations, different gifts.
This block began with the first of them, and today it closes with both.

teach.h: BHAI GURDAS: THE SCRIBE AND HIS VARS.
teach.b: Walk back through what they gave. Bhai Gurdas first: the scribe of the Granth, tradition says, who kept his own vars beside the book and never inside it.
In his vars, the world before Nanak, and the mist clearing when Nanak came. The debate at Achal. The cup of milk at Multan with the jasmine flower floating on it.
The Guru bowing to his disciple. A roll of honor, ordinary Sikhs remembered by name and town. A Sikh's day from early rising to honest work.
One Sikh, two a sangat, five where the Lord is present.

teach.h: BHAI NAND LAL: THE POET AT COURT.
teach.b: Then Bhai Nand Lal, the Persian poet at Guru Gobind Singh's court. His book of life, longing to see the Beloved in everything. His ghazals, still sung.
The rehat writings attributed to him, which historians discuss. And this week, the story of his kitchen, where a stranger was fed at the wrong hour. What joins them?

teach.h: NEITHER A RIVAL TO THE GURU.
teach.b: Neither tried to become the Guru's rival.

teach.h: GIFTS SPENT MAKING THE WORD CLEAR.
teach.b: Bhai Gurdas wrote out the Guru's word and kept his own off the page; Nand Lal poured his gifts into praise. That's why the Sikh code of conduct lets their words be sung beside Gurbani: they explain it, not replace it.

They were servants of the Word, the Guru's word, the Shabad. And servant doesn't mean small here. Both were gifted men, and their whole skill went into making the Guru's word clearer for someone else.
Next week, the stories of Nanak's own life, the janamsakhis: different tellers, different tellings. These two make a good pair to hold the new tellers beside.

how: Sikhs read and sing the works of Bhai Gurdas and Bhai Nand Lal as companions to Gurbani; the Sikh code of conduct allows them in kirtan because they explain the Guru's word.

o: a poet's own verses about the Gurus
the Guru's word, sung as a hymn
a short prayer said at sunrise

games.q: the two tellers — tap the pairs.
p: the cup of milk at Multan
the kitchen open at any hour

s: Bhai Gurdas and Bhai Nand Lal wrote in the same language
Bhai Gurdas wrote in Punjabi and Braj; Bhai Nand Lal wrote in Persian.
both tellers' works may be sung in kirtan
the Sikh code of conduct allows them because they explain Gurbani.

games.q: you're Bhai Gurdas, writing out the Guru's hymns for the Granth. your own vars are loved too. where do they go?
o: into the Granth, beside the hymns.
outside the Granth, as a key to it.
games.why: tradition remembers the scribe keeping his own vars off the page; they're sung beside Gurbani because they explain it, the mark of a servant of the Word.

practice: Bring to mind one teller in your life, a grandparent with stories, a teacher who made a hard thing clear, the person who taught you a recipe, a prayer or a song, and hold their face for a moment.
Remember one thing they told you, in their words if you can, and if they're gone, say their name softly. If you pray, you can say Waheguru for them.

wordCard.voice: Shabad, the Guru's word both Bhai Gurdas and Bhai Nand Lal, a scribe and a poet, put their gifts in service of.

orig.note: shabad: the Guru's word, the Word both tellers served.

carryVoice: Your line: servants of the word. Gifted men, every gift spent on the Guru's word. Two tellers, one block, closed.
